summary: Defines a Sieve extension that lets a copy of a message generated by an action be filed into a target mailbox. It adds a new tagged argument to the Vacation and Notify actions, updating RFC 5230 and RFC 5435. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When your email filter sends an automatic reply, you may want to keep a copy. This adds a way to tuck that copy into a folder.

questions: how to save a copy of a vacation reply in sieve
what does the sieve fcc argument do
subtitle: How a Sieve mail filter can keep a copy of the automatic replies and notifications it sends for you.

tldr.problem: Sieve actions such as vacation and notify can generate extra messages on the user's behalf, but the user has no standard way to keep an archive of what was sent.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds an optional :fcc tagged argument that names a mailbox, and the Sieve interpreter files a copy of the generated message there, wrapped in Internet Message Format if needed.
tldr.outcome: The extension is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5230 and RFC 5435; it is forbidden with reject and ereject, and filing copies can use up quota or expose information in shared mailboxes.

today: RFC 8580 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5230 and RFC 5435 by adding the :fcc argument to Vacation and Notify.

sections.title: Why Keep Copies of Generated Mail
sections.content:
The Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228) has action commands, and some of them generate additional messages on behalf of the user. An auto-reply sent while someone is on holiday is the usual example. It is sometimes desirable for the user to keep an archive of those generated messages.

This RFC defines :fcc (File Carbon Copy), a new optional tagged argument for such actions. It tells the Sieve interpreter to file a copy of the generated message into a target mailbox. The capability string for the extension is fcc, so a script must list it in its require line.

Each future action that generates messages has to say how it interacts with FCC. This document does so for Vacation (RFC 5230) and Notify (RFC 5435).
sections.eli5: Sometimes your mail robot writes letters for you. This gives it a way to put a copy of each letter in a folder so you can look at it later.

sections.title: The :fcc Tagged Argument
sections.content:
The usage is :fcc <mailbox: string>. The mailbox argument is treated like the mailbox argument of the fileinto action in RFC 5228. An invalid mailbox name MAY be treated as an error or lead to delivery to an implementation-defined mailbox. If the mailbox does not exist, the implementation MAY treat that as an error, create it, or file the message into an implementation-defined mailbox.

Three options from other extensions can be combined with :fcc, and each one behaves as it does with fileinto. The matching extension MUST be enabled when it is used.

  • :flags (Imap4flags) sets the given IMAP flags when the copy is filed.
  • :create (Mailbox) creates the target mailbox first, if needed.
  • :specialuse (Special-Use) files the copy into a mailbox that carries the given special-use flag if one exists, and otherwise into the target mailbox.

The RFC gives an ABNF rule: FCC = ":fcc" string *FCC-OPTS. The options may appear in any order, and each MUST NOT appear more than once.
sections.eli5: You write the folder name after the word fcc. You can also say to make the folder if it is missing, or to mark the copy as already read.

sections.title: Format of Filed Copies
sections.content:
Copies filed through this extension are REQUIRED to be in Internet Message Format (RFC 5322). Some generated messages already are, and MAY be filed unchanged. Messages in other formats MUST be encapsulated using Internet Message Format and MIME constructs.

The general encapsulation rules are:

  • Date: REQUIRED, and SHOULD be the time the message was generated.
  • From: REQUIRED, and SHOULD be the email address of the owner of the Sieve script. The RFC quotes an erratum advising that if the owner has several addresses, the one seen in the To or Cc fields of the incoming message is the better choice.
  • To: OPTIONAL; may be the recipient of the generated message.
  • Subject: OPTIONAL; may be Fcc: followed by the subject of the message being processed.
  • In-Reply-To: OPTIONAL; may be the Message-ID of the message being processed.
  • Message body: REQUIRED, made of one or more MIME parts holding the generated message and any related metadata, with Content-Type set to the proper types and Content-Transfer-Encoding set if any part has 8-bit or binary data.
sections.eli5: The copy has to look like a proper email, with a date, a sender and a body, so any mail program can open it from the folder.

sections.title: Vacation and Notify Actions
sections.content:
For vacation, the FCC argument is added to the usage line, so the auto-reply can be stored in a mailbox. Vacation replies already comply with MIME, so they can be filed without modification. The RFC example sends a seven-day vacation reply and files the copy into INBOX.Sent with the flag \\Seen.

For notify, FCC is likewise an optional argument. Messages made with the mailto method are MIME-compliant and can be filed as they are. Messages from other methods, such as xmpp, MUST be encapsulated as described in the format section. The filed body MUST include the :message argument and MAY include :from, :importance or :options.

An implementation MAY support FCC only for some of its notification methods, and using it with an unsupporting method is an error. Scripts can check at run time with the new notification-capability fcc in the notify_method_capability test, which matches yes or no.
sections.eli5: The robot that answers while you are away, and the robot that pings you about new mail, can both keep a copy. A script can first ask a pinging method whether it can keep copies.

sections.title: Actions That Cannot Use FCC
sections.content:
Implementations MUST NOT allow FCC with the reject and ereject actions (RFC 5429). Allowing it would break the SMTP principle that a message is either delivered or bounced back to the sender, because the saved copy of the rejection would contain the original message. Using :fcc there is an error.

More generally, FCC is not compatible with any Sieve action that does not generate an additional message for the user, and using it with such an action is an error. Future actions that generate messages need to describe how they work with FCC and how to MIME-encapsulate their output.
sections.eli5: A copy only makes sense for letters the robot writes. If the robot is bouncing a letter back, keeping a copy would mean keeping the other person's letter, which is not allowed.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
On top of the considerations in the earlier Sieve, Vacation, Notify and Seconds RFCs, the security section adds one point: filing copies of generated messages may push the script owner over the allocated storage quota on the mail system, which would prevent delivery of future messages.

The privacy section warns about shared or public mailboxes. A copy filed there could expose private information about the script owner to third parties. For instance, other users of the mailbox might learn that the owner is on holiday or learn the owner's physical location.
sections.eli5: If the copy folder gets full, new mail may stop arriving. And if the folder is shared with others, they could read your copies and learn that you are away.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the Sieve extension fcc in the Sieve Extensions registry, described as adding the :fcc parameter to Sieve action commands that generate additional messages. The contact is the Sieve discussion list.

IANA also registered a notification-capability parameter named fcc. It reports whether a copy of a notification sent with a given method can be filed into a target mailbox. Its value is yes or no, and values MUST be in lowercase.
sections.eli5: The new word and the new yes-or-no question were written in the official lists so nobody else uses them for something different.
